title: Numbers
scope_note: Proposed original curriculum. The supplied college material shows a Numbers chapter on page 7; chapter content has not been provided or reviewed.

skills.title: Integers, parity and number properties
skills.objective: Classify integers and reason about odd and even numbers.
skills.lesson: An integer is even when it is divisible by 2, including zero and negative multiples of 2. Other integers are odd. Test a claim with examples, then explain it using 2k or 2k+1.

skills.title: Divisibility rules
skills.objective: Apply divisibility rules and combine conditions.
skills.lesson: A number is divisible by 3 or 9 when its digit sum is divisible by 3 or 9. Divisibility by 6 requires divisibility by both 2 and 3. Applying only one necessary condition is insufficient.

skills.title: Primes, composites and factors
skills.objective: Recognize prime numbers and enumerate positive factors.
skills.lesson: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors. One is neither prime nor composite. Pair factors around the square root; count the square root only once for perfect squares.

skills.title: HCF and LCM
skills.objective: Distinguish common factors from common multiples and apply each in context.
skills.lesson: HCF is the greatest positive common factor; LCM is the least positive common multiple. Equal groups without leftovers typically use HCF; simultaneous repeating events typically use LCM. For positive integers a and b, HCF(a,b) times LCM(a,b) equals a times b.

skills.title: Remainders
skills.objective: Use quotient-remainder form and simplify powers modulo a positive divisor.
skills.lesson: For an integer n and positive divisor d, write n = dq+r with 0 <= r < d. Reduce factors before multiplying. A remainder is constrained by the divisor and is not the decimal part of division.

skills.title: Place value and units-digit cycles
skills.objective: Use place value and repeated units-digit patterns.
skills.lesson: The units digit is the remainder modulo 10. Powers of 2 end in 2,4,8,6 and repeat. An exponent divisible by the cycle length uses the last position of the cycle, not the first.
